titel: The gold standard and gold as an investment
kurz: How a self-imposed commitment to gold turned into a monetary system based on trust alone, and what return gold has delivered since then.

bloecke.md:
A [[gold standard]] is a self-imposed commitment by the state and not a statement about a metal. The state promises to exchange its currency unit for gold at a fixed rate at any time, and in doing so gives up control over the money supply. If gold flows into the country, the money supply grows, and if gold is withdrawn, it shrinks. The exchange rate between two gold currencies then follows arithmetically from the ratio of their parities. There is no exchange rate policy, because there is nothing to decide.

Under the classical gold standard between about 1870 and 1914, adjustment worked through the mechanism that David Hume had described in the 18th century. A country with a balance of payments deficit loses gold, its money supply shrinks, prices and wages fall, and exports become competitive again. Adjustment therefore takes place through the domestic economy and not through the exchange rate. The system rests on this, and this is also where its costs lie, because the burden falls on working people.

bloecke.titel: The political basis of the gold standard
bloecke.md: The classical gold standard held because hardly anyone was able to make the costs of deflation count politically, and not because metal money is more honest than paper money. Trade unions were weak, the franchise was limited, and full employment was not a government objective. As soon as mass suffrage and an organised labour movement came along, the self-imposed commitment became untenable. This is the central argument of Barry Eichengreen's *Golden Fetters*. A gold standard is therefore less an economic decision than a constitutional one about who pays in a crisis.

## The return to gold between the wars

The First World War ended convertibility everywhere, because no country wanted to make its war financing dependent on its gold reserves. The return after the war failed. In 1925 Britain tied the pound to gold again at the pre-war parity. This rate overvalued the currency and brought the country deflation, wage disputes and, in 1926, the General Strike. In 1931 London abandoned the peg. In 1933 the US banned private individuals from owning gold, and in 1934 it devalued the dollar from $20.67 to $35 per fine ounce. Economic history shows clearly that countries that left the gold standard early emerged from the Great Depression sooner. In the Depression, the gold peg offered no protection; it constrained monetary policy and held back the recovery.

bloecke.titel: Milestones from the gold standard to the present
bloecke.unter: Six of the ten milestones mark a point at which a self-imposed commitment failed because of its political costs.

bloecke.md:
## Bretton Woods 1944

In July 1944, delegations from 44 states agreed in Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, on a weakened version, a gold exchange standard. Only the dollar was tied to gold, at $35 per fine ounce. It could be redeemed by foreign central banks alone, not by private individuals. All other currencies were pegged to the dollar with a fluctuation band of about 1%. Changes in parity were only envisaged in the event of a fundamental disequilibrium and with the agreement of the newly founded International Monetary Fund.

Capital controls were a deliberate part of the construction. Only as long as capital did not flow freely could fixed exchange rates and an independent national interest rate policy be achieved at the same time. Keynes's proposal for a supranational unit of account did not prevail. The world currency became the dollar, and thus the currency of a single state with its own domestic political interests.

Around 1960, Robert Triffin described a contradiction that was built into the system. The growing world economy needed more and more dollars as a reserve and trading currency. It could only obtain these dollars if the US permanently sent more money abroad than it got back. As a result, foreign dollar claims grew faster than the American gold stock, and the promise of convertibility lost credibility.

The [[Triffin dilemma]] allows no way out. If the US supplies too few dollars, world trade suffers from a lack of liquidity. If it supplies enough, gold backing becomes ever smaller. In the 1960s, foreign dollar claims exceeded US gold reserves. The London Gold Pool, through which several central banks held the market price at $35, collapsed in March 1968. After that, two gold prices existed side by side: the official one for central banks and a free market price.

## The Nixon shock of 1971

After a three-day retreat at Camp David, Nixon announced on the evening of 15 August 1971 that the dollar's convertibility into gold would be suspended. This was accompanied by a wage and price freeze and an import surcharge of 10%. The Smithsonian Agreement of December 1971 made one more attempt to maintain fixed exchange rates, now with the dollar devalued to $38 per fine ounce. In March 1973 this attempt was also abandoned. Since then, the major currencies have floated freely against each other, and the suspension announced in 1971 as *temporary* remains in force to this day.

Since 1971, no major currency has been backed by metal; the value of currencies is safeguarded by institutions. The discipline of the system rests on mandate, independence and credibility and no longer on physical holdings. This is less strict, but it makes it possible to respond to a recession with falling interest rates instead of falling wages.

The transition was not smooth. With the end of the gold peg, monetary policy in the 1970s had lost its orientation and had not yet found a new one. The oil price shock of 1973 hit a system without a rule. Instead of a return to metal, substitutes emerged: first money supply targets, later a numerical inflation target and legally independent central banks. At the same time, the exchange rate risk that the state had previously borne passed to companies and investors. The currency risk of every foreign currency investment in a portfolio is a consequence of this changeover in 1973.

## Gold as money and as an investment

Gold has not proved itself as money. It is used as a medium of exchange practically nowhere, because the transaction costs are disproportionately high. Nor does it serve as a unit of account, because in Germany neither a wage nor a rent nor a supermarket price is stated in grams of gold. That leaves the function of a store of value, and whether gold fulfils it can be tested against data.

bloecke.md: Every figure in the table is correct, but depending on the starting point it leads to a different conclusion. The 5% real return since 1971 is biased upwards, because the starting value of $35 was a price set by the state and not a market price. Calculated from a market price, the result is between -15.0% and +8.6% a year in real terms, depending on the start and end year.

Buyer A buys an ounce for $850 in January 1980. In 2026 prices, he has thus committed around $3,660 of purchasing power. Today the ounce is worth $4,416, a real gain of around 21% in 46 years, or 0.4% a year. An unspectacular investment with a real interest rate of 2% would have grown the stake to two and a half times its value in real terms over the same period.

Buyer B buys at the end of 2000 for $272. He earns 8.6% a year in real terms, more than most stock markets over this period.

Both own the same asset and need the same storage space; the only difference is the entry price. Since gold does not generate a cash flow, it has no intrinsic value towards which the price could gradually move back after an unfavourable entry. The only thing that counts is the price at the time of the later sale.

bloecke.titel: Gold's share of official reserves at current and earlier prices
bloecke.unter: At the end of 2025, gold was ahead of the euro at 27%; calculated at end-2023 prices, the two would be level.

bloecke.md: The gold price rose by around 27% in 2024 and by around 65% in 2025. A large part of gold's much-cited rise in central bank balance sheets is therefore due to valuation and not to reallocation. Nevertheless, central banks bought around 860 tonnes of gold in 2025. In addition, there was private investment demand of around 2,200 tonnes, almost twice as much as in the previous year.

links.titel: Arguments for gold in a portfolio
punkte: Physical gold is not a liability of an issuer or debtor and therefore has no default risk.
Gold has different price drivers from equities and bonds. Its correlation is close to zero on average, which reduces the fluctuations of the portfolio.
Historically, gold has proved its worth where payment promises failed, for example in currency reforms, capital controls and state bankruptcies.
Central banks buy for political reasons and not for the return; as buyers they pay little attention to the price.

rechts.titel: Arguments against gold in a portfolio
punkte: Gold pays neither interest nor dividends nor rent. The entire return consists of price changes and therefore depends on expectations about the expectations of other investors.
Periods of real losses lasting twenty years and more are documented, for example from 1980 to 2000 with a real loss of around 86%.
There is no valuation yardstick. Without a cash flow, it is impossible to say whether $4,416 is expensive or cheap.
In addition, there are costs for the premium when buying small denominations, for storage and insurance, and the spread when selling back.
There is currency risk, because gold is quoted in dollars but the investor calculates in euros.

bloecke.md:
## The real interest rate as the most important price driver

Because gold pays out nothing, holding it costs as much as a safe investment yields in real terms. If the real interest rate falls, this opportunity cost falls and gold becomes more attractive. If it rises, the reverse applies. Statistically, this is the most stable explanation for gold price movements, but it only explains part of them.

In September 2026 the limits of this model become apparent. The ECB deposit facility rate is 2.50%, and German inflation was 2.9% in August. In the short term, the real interest rate is therefore slightly negative, while at long maturities the opposite is true. At around 3.5%, ten-year German federal bonds (Bunds) are yielding more than at any time since 2011 and are clearly above the inflation rate. According to the real interest rate model, gold ought to be under pressure. It is indeed trading around a fifth below its record high of the end of January 2026, but still around two thirds above its level at the end of 2024. The model does not capture demand for insurance against political risks, because this cannot be put into an equation.

bloecke.titel: Forms of investment and taxes in 2026
bloecke.md:
- Physical **[[investment gold]]** (bars and investment coins) is exempt from VAT. Silver, platinum and collector coins are not. The premium on small denominations can amount to several per cent and represents an immediate loss relative to the spot price.
- Gains from physical gold are a private disposal transaction (privates Veräußerungsgeschäft) under Section 23 EStG (Income Tax Act). After a holding period of more than one year they are tax-free. Before that, they are taxed in full at the personal tax rate as soon as the total gain from all private disposal transactions in the year reaches the exemption threshold (Freigrenze) of €1,000.
- Xetra-Gold is a bearer bond with a claim to physical delivery and was backed by 172.8 tonnes at the end of 2025. According to the case law of the Federal Fiscal Court (BFH), it is treated like physical gold for tax purposes and is therefore tax-free after one year, unlike almost any other security.
- This information describes the legal position and is not a recommendation. What determines the taxation is the legal form and not the prospectus.

“Gold protects against inflation.” Over very long periods this is roughly true, but over normal investment horizons it often is not. In the inflation years 2021 and 2022, gold lost slightly in nominal terms while prices rose. In real terms, a loss therefore arose precisely when the protection was needed.

“Gold is safe.” Safe here means free of default risk, but not stable in value. Historically, gold's volatility has been of the same order as that of a broad equity index, at around 17% a year.

“The Nixon shock was the beginning of the end of money.” Since 1971 the purchasing power of the Deutsche Mark and the euro has declined considerably, while real incomes and productivity have risen at the same time. The gold peg did not prevent losses of prosperity. It distributed them differently, as deflation and unemployment instead of gradual currency debasement.

mitnehmen: A gold standard determines who bears the burden of adjustment in a crisis, and it is no guarantee of stable money.
Bretton Woods failed because of a contradiction in its construction, the Triffin dilemma, since a currency cannot be a reserve currency and remain backed at the same time.
Since 1971, the value of money has rested on institutions instead of metal, that is on the mandate, independence and credibility of central banks.
Gold has not proved itself as money, and as an investment it generates no cash flow, so the return depends almost entirely on the entry price.
Real returns on gold range from minus 15.0% to plus 8.6% a year depending on the start and end year, and every single one of these figures rests on a choice of period.

begriffe.text: Monetary order in which the central bank redeems its currency in gold at a fixed rate. The money supply therefore follows gold holdings. Balance of payments imbalances are corrected through falling domestic prices and wages instead of through the exchange rate.

International monetary order agreed in 1944. The dollar was tied to gold at $35 per fine ounce and convertible only for central banks; all other currencies were pegged to the dollar within narrow bands. The system ended de facto in 1971 and formally in 1973.

Announcement of 15 August 1971 suspending the dollar's convertibility into gold, combined with a wage and price freeze and an import surcharge. Since then, the international monetary system has been based on pure fiat money without metal backing and on floating exchange rates.

The contradiction that a country whose currency is the world reserve currency can only supply the world with liquidity through persistent balance of payments deficits. Precisely by doing so, it weakens the backing and credibility of its currency.

Gold in the form of bars or investment coins with a statutory minimum fineness. It is exempt from VAT in the EU. In Germany, gains on disposal are tax-free after a holding period of more than one year.
